huddle.e: From Middle English *hudelen, alteration (due to hudels, hidels (“hiding place”), see hiddle) of *huderen, hoderen (“to cover; press together; huddle”), a frequentative form of Middle English huden, hiden (“to hide”), equivalent to hide + -le and/or hide + -er.
huddle.g: A small group of individuals in very close proximity to one another.

hug.e: From earlier hugge (“to embrace, clasp with the arms”) (1560), probably representing a conflation of huck (“to crouch, huddle down”) and Old Norse hugga (“to comfort, console”), from hugr (“mind, heart, thought”).
hug.g: A close embrace, especially when charged with an emotion such as affection, joy, relief, lust, anger, aggression, compassion, or the like, a

huge.e: From Middle English huge, from Old French ahuge (“high, lofty, great, large, huge”), of unknown origin. One theory derives it from an underlying Old French a hoge (“at height”), from a (“at, to”) + hoge (“a hill, height”), the latter from Frankish *haug or cognate Old Norse haugr (“hill”); both from Proto-Germanic *haugaz (“hill, mound”).

human.e: From Late Middle English humaigne, humayne, humain, from Middle French humain, from Old French humain, umain (“of or belonging to man”, adjective), from Latin hūmānus m (“of man, human”, adjective).
human.g: Of or belonging to the species Homo sapiens or its closest relatives.

humanity.e: From Middle English humanyte, humanite, humanitye, from Old French humanité, from Latin hūmānitās. By surface analysis, human or humane + -ity. Partly displaced mankind, from Old English mancynn (literally “human race”).
humanity.g: Humankind; human beings as a group.

humble.e: From Middle English humble, from Old French humble, umble, humle, from Latin humilis (“low, slight, hence mean, humble”) (compare Greek χαμηλός (khamēlós, “on the ground, low, trifling”)), from humus (“the earth, ground”), humi (“on the ground”).
humble.g: Not pretentious or magnificent; unpretending; unassuming.

humble.e: From Middle English *humblen, *humbelen (suggested by humblynge (“a humming, a faint rumbling”)), frequentative of Middle English hummen (“to hum”), equivalent to hum + -le.

humbleness.e: From Middle English humblenesse; equivalent to humble + -ness.
humbleness.g: Modesty, humility; the property of being humble.

humbly.e: From Middle English humbely, humbliche. By surface analysis, humble + -ly.

humiliate.e: Borrowed from Late Latin humiliātus, perfect passive participle of humiliō (“to abase, humble”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin humilis (“lowly, humble”), from humus (“ground; earth, soil”); see humble.
humiliate.g: To cause to be ashamed; to injure the dignity and self-respect of.

humiliation.e: From Middle French humiliation, from Late Latin humiliātiō, from humiliāre (“to humiliate”); see humiliate. Equivalent to humiliate + -ion.
humiliation.g: The act of humiliating or humbling someone; abasement of pride; mortification.

humility.e: From Middle English humilite, from Old French (h)umilité, from Latin humilitas (“lowness, meanness, baseness, in Late Latin humility”), from humilis (“low, lowly, humble, earth”). Equivalent to humble + -ity, with /mb/ reduced to /m/ (compare plumbing).
humility.g: The characteristic of being humble; humbleness in character and behavior.

hump.e: Probably borrowed from Dutch homp (“hump, lump”) or Middle Low German hump (“heap, hill, stump”), from Old Saxon *hump (“hill, heap, thick piece”), from Proto-Germanic *humpaz (“hip, height”), from Proto-Indo-European *kumb- (“curved”). Replaced, and perhaps influenced by, Old English crump (“crooked, bent”).

hunch.e: Assibilated variant of hunk, of uncertain origin. Alternatively, a derivative of hump, via an earlier Middle English *hunche, *humpchin, from *hump + -chin, -chen (diminutive suffix), equivalent to hump + -kin.

hunchback.g: One who is stooped or hunched over.

hundred.e: From Middle English hundred, from Old English hundred, from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”), a neuter variant of *radō (“row, line, series”).
hundred.g: A numerical value equal to 100 (10²), occurring after ninety-nine; ten times ten.

hundredfold.e: From Middle English hundredfold. Equivalent to hundred + -fold.

hundredth.e: From Middle English hundred (“hundredth”); equivalent to and remodelled after hundred + -th (ordinal suffix), displacing Old English hundtēontigoþa.
hundredth.g: The ordinal form of the number one hundred.

hunger.e: From Middle English hunger, from Old English hungor (“hunger, desire; famine”), from Proto-West Germanic *hungr, from Proto-Germanic *hungruz, *hunhruz (“hunger”), from Proto-Indo-European *kenk- (“to burn, smart, desire, hunger, thirst”).
hunger.g: A need or compelling desire for food.

hunger.e: From Middle English hungren, from Old English hyngran, hyngrian, ġehyngrian (“to be hungry”), from Proto-West Germanic *hungrijan, from Proto-Germanic *hungrijaną.
hunger.g: To be in need of food.

hungry.e: From Middle English hungry, from Old English hungriġ, from Proto-West Germanic *hungrug, from Proto-Germanic *hungrugaz (“hungry”); equivalent to hunger + -y.
hungry.g: Affected by hunger; having the physical need for food.

hunt.e: From Middle English hunten, from Old English huntian (“to hunt”), from Proto-West Germanic *huntōn (“to hunt, capture”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱent- (“to catch, seize”). In some areas read as a collective form of hound by folk etymology.
hunt.g: To find or search for an animal in the wild with the intention of killing the animal for its meat or for sport.

hunter.e: From Middle English huntere, hunter, equivalent to hunt + -er.
hunter.g: One who hunts game for sport or for food; a huntsman or huntswoman.

hunting.e: From Middle English huntynge, alteration of earlier Middle English huntinde, huntende, huntand, present participle of hunten (“to hunt”), equivalent to hunt + -ing.

hurl.e: From Middle English hurlen, of onomatopoeic origin; compare hurry, hurtle.

hurry.e: From Middle English horien (“to rush, impel”), probably a variation of hurren (“to vibrate rapidly, buzz”), from Proto-Germanic *hurzaną (“to rush”) (compare Middle High German hurren (“to hasten”), Norwegian hurre (“to whirl around”)).

hurt.e: From Middle English hurten, hirten, hertan (“to injure, scathe, knock together”), from Old Northern French hurter ("to ram into, strike, collide with"; > Modern French heurter), perhaps from Frankish *hūrt (“a battering ram”), cognate with Welsh hwrdd (“ram”) and Cornish hordh (“ram”).
hurt.g: To cause (a person or animal) physical pain and/or injury.

hurt.e: Unclear. Suggestions include: from its resemblance to a blue hurtleberry, or from French heurt (a blow, leaving a blue bruise), the latter of which would make it a doublet of hurt Etymology 1; compare the theories about golpe (“purple roundel”)).

hurtful.g: Tending to impair or damage; injurious; occasioning loss or injury.

husband.e: From Middle English husbonde, from Old English hūsbonda, from hūs + bonda. Calque of Old Norse húsbóndi. By surface analysis, house + bond.
husband.g: A man in a marriage or marital relationship, especially in relation to his spouse.

husbandman.e: From Middle English husbandman, husbondman, equivalent to husband + -man.
husbandman.g: a person who raises crops and tends animals; a farmer

husbandry.e: From Middle English hus-bō̆ndrī, hus-bō̆ndrīe, husbanderi, husbonderie, housbondrye, housebondrie (“household management, housekeeping; household duties; economy, skilful management, thrift; farm management, agriculture, farming; cultivation; household articles; husbands collectively”), from hǒus-bō̆nd, hǒus-bō̆nde (“male spouse, husband; master of a house.
husbandry.g: The occupation or work of a husbandman or farmer; the cultivation of crops and the raising of livestock; agriculture.

hush.e: From Middle English huschen (“to hush”) (as past participle husht (“silent; hushed”) and interjection husht (“quiet!”)).

husk.e: From Middle English huske, husk (“husk”). Perhaps from Old English *husuc, *hosuc (“little covering, sheath”), diminutive of hosu (“pod, shell, husk”), from Proto-West Germanic *hosā, from Proto-Germanic *husǭ (“covering, shell, leggings”), from Proto-Indo-European *kawəs- / kawes- (“cover”). If so, equivalent to hose + -ock.
husk.g: The dry, leafy or stringy exterior of certain vegetables or fruits, which must be removed before eating the meat inside.

husk.e: Partly imitative, partly from Etymology 1, above, influenced by husky.
husk.g: An infection in cattle caused by a species of Dictyocaulus or lungworm

hut.e: From Middle English *hutte, hotte, from both Old English hōd and Old English hȳdan (“to hide”) and influenced by Anglo-Norman hute or hutte, from Middle French hutte, from Old French hute (“hut”), hute (“cottage”), from Old High German hutta (“hut, cottage”), from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ, *hudjō (“hut”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewt- (“to deck; cover.
hut.g: A small, simple one-storey dwelling or shelter, often with just one room, and generally built of readily available local materials.

hut.e: A short, sharp sound of command.
hut.g: Called by the quarterback to prepare the team for a play.

hang.e: From Middle English hangen, hongen, from a fusion of Old English hōn (“to hang, be hanging”, transitive verb) and hangian (“to hang, cause to hang”, intransitive verb), respectively from the transitive verb Proto-West Germanic *hą̄han and the intransitive verb *hangēn.
From hang sangwich, Irish colloquial pronunciation of ham sandwich.
hang.g: Cheap processed ham (cured pork), often made specially for sandwiches.
